g.text: ADR-001: Match Bruckner's reviewers; publish at 99% verdict confidence
Status: accepted
Session: S1
Cards: 01
Exam: P1 · P6
Supersedes: none
Superseded by: none
Question
one sentence
For the results check, when are our verdicts good enough, and which verdicts may be published without a person approving them?
Context
what forces this decision now: facts and constraints, no solutions
Bruckner et al. reviewed CTIS as exported on 2025-11-10 (7,547 Phase II–IV trials, now seeded in ctis.search_export_snapshot). Of 234 trials legally required to report: 116 reported fully on time, 20
late, 98 not fully reported. Of the 234, 140 had a complete results document, 47 an incomplete one, 47 none. Two people checked each of 206 results documents (participants reported, outcomes

reported, cancelled); they first agreed on 163 and resolved the rest. Their "extended deadline" flags came from non-public CTIS data. A wrong "not fully reported" accuses a named sponsor in public. An
LLM's own confidence number is not calibrated out of the box.
Options
2–3 real options; the current proposal is only one of them
A. Match the reviewers, then publish at ≥ 99% confidence
(chosen)
How it works: run the workflow on the 2025-11-10 snapshot
until every disagreement with the reviewers is explained. Each
verdict carries an internal confidence; below 99% it needs
manual approval.
Pros:
• a published, human-made bar to measure against
• unsure verdicts wait for a person
• the 99% line is set on real labels
Cons:
• results documents must be fetched as they were
• 47 incomplete documents is a small test set
B. A person approves every verdict
How it works: nothing is published until someone has approved
it, whatever the confidence.
Pros:
• no unreviewed verdict is ever published
Cons:
• review work grows with every trial
• confidence is never put to the test
C. One threshold, no manual approval
How it works: publish verdicts at or above a threshold; drop
everything below it.
Pros:
• no review work at all
Cons:
• borderline cases vanish silently
• one wrong threshold puts errors in public
Criteria × options
+ better · 0 no difference · – worse, and a few words why
Criterion
Option A
Option B
Option C
Quality: verdicts we can stand behind
+ measured against human reviewers
+ every verdict seen by a person
– nothing checked by a person
Cost: my review time per week
+ only verdicts under 99%
– every verdict
+ none
Risk: harm from a wrong verdict
+ low; unsure verdicts wait
+ low, if review keeps up
– wrong verdicts go public
Effort: to build and maintain
0 comparison + approval queue
0 approval queue
+ one threshold
Undo: how hard to change later
+ the 99% line is a config value
0 dropping approval is a rework
0 adding approval is a rework
Learning: what it teaches us
+ calibration on real labels
– confidence never measured
– no feedback loop
Decision
what we chose and which criteria decided it
We choose A. Development gate: run our workflow on Bruckner's 2025-11-10 snapshot and compare with the reviewers' final labels, per trial and per part (participants, outcomes,
cancelled), until every disagreement is explained as our bug (fixed), data that changed after their review (set aside) or a likely labelling error (noted). Extended deadlines come from
Bruckner's flag, because they used non-public data.
Each verdict carries a verdict confidence from 0 to 100%: our model's internal certainty about that one trial's verdict. At 99% or above it may be published; below 99% it needs manual
approval. The 99% line is set during this development: verdicts we score at 99% or above must match the reviewers at least 99% of the time. Every verdict stores its decision record:
verdict; confidence; per-part results with quote and page; threshold and config version; model id and prompt version; a short reason.
Consequences
We measure progress against one published, human-made answer key. Moving the publish line is
a config change. Review time goes only to verdicts under 99%. Any verdict can be explained from
its own record.
Results documents must be fetched as they were when the reviewers read them. With 47
incomplete documents, Bruckner's data alone can't prove the 99% line. Confidence must be
re-checked whenever the model or prompt changes.
Revisit when · Lab
Verdicts at 99% or above match the reviewers or manual approvals less than 99% of the time. Or
a published verdict turns out wrong. Or a second labelled dataset disagrees with Bruckner's
reviewers. Or the publication policy (S13) changes who approves what.
Done: their export, PIP list, final verdicts and per-part reviews loaded (ctis seed, gold
bruckner, gold bruckner-reviews); our due-date rules reproduce all 277 verdicts (gold
compare-due). Accepted 2026-11-01. The per-part comparison and setting the 99% line on real
confidence scores move to S8's lab, once the results-document check exists.
Session notes
optional
The reviewers first agreed on 79% of documents, so 100% raw agreement isn't expected; the 43 they argued about are good tests for low confidence. Rule of three: showing ≤ 1% error takes about
300 correct high-confidence verdicts in a row, more than Bruckner's set, so manual approvals keep adding labels until then. How the confidence is produced is decided in S5 and S7.

How to use: copy to docs/adr/ADR-NNN-name.excalidraw · replace the grey text (set it to black) · status chip colour: orange open, yellow proposed, green accepted, grey superseded · one page: if it doesn't fit, the decision
is too big, so split it.
